newsitem.title: USA: Open-air U.S. A-bomb tests may cause thyroid cancer.
newsitem.headline: Open-air U.S. A-bomb tests may cause thyroid cancer.

text.p: Radioactive fallout could produce thyroid cancers in 10,000 to 75,000 Americans who were younger than 15 during the atomic bomb tests of the 1950s and '60s, the National Cancer Institute said on Friday.

Results of a nationwide study showed people in Western states to the north and east of the Nevada test site had the most exposure. But everyone in the 48 contiguous states was exposed at some level for about two months following each of the 90 atmospheric tests.
"Hot spots" dotted the West and Midwest, determined by rainfall, grazing patterns of livestock, whether the people drank locally produced milk, and other factors.

Children aged 3 months to 5 years probably received three to seven times the average dose for the population in their county because they drank more milk than adults and their thyroids were smaller, the study said.
In contrast, it said, most adults probably received two to four times less than the average county dose.
Nearly all of the projected increased cancers would be in people who were younger than 15 at the time of exposure, and about 75 percent of the cases would be in people who were under five.

The study said the average cumulative thyroid dose to the approximately 160 million people in the country at the time was about 2 rads, which is about five times the amount of radiation given by a modern mammogram.
In the 24 counties with the highest exposures, estimated average cumulative doses ranged from 9 to 16 rads.

Calculating cancer risks from various exposures levels is still not possible, although the Chernobyl disaster provided an unfortunate laboratory for study, NCI director Richard Klausner said in a telephone briefing.
"We don't have the data to say there was a large risk, yet we can't rule it out," Klausner said.
Thyroid cancer rates in Belarus and Ukraine, which received the heaviest radiation doses from the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster, have climbed and are under intensive study.

Radioactive iodine concentrates in the thyroid gland. This year, about 16,100 Americans will be diagnosed with thyroid cancer and 1,230 will die from it. The incidence for women is more than two times higher than for men, the study said.

The National Academy of Sciences' Institute of Medicine will review the NCI study to assess risks to individuals and make recommedations to doctors on how to treat people with elevated risks because of fallout exposure.
People who are concerned that they had high exposures should consult with their doctors, Klausner said.
The full 1,000-page study and accompanying 100,000 pages of data are to be released on the Internet in October, with a listing of areas with high exposure.

Congress ordered the study in 1982 after publicity about "downwinders," people in Utah downwind of the Nevada test site. It has been in the works since 1984 and involved calculating meteorological records, cattle grazing patterns and other factors to figure doses.
Critics complained that the study took an unreasonably long time and people were kept at risk awaiting the findings. But Klausner defended the project, saying it was an immensely complex undertaking.

"We are moving to get all of the information out as quickly as we can. Not knowing what risk these exposures actually convey to individual, we don't know what getting this information out a year ago or two years ago could have done," he said.
The National Committee for Radiation Victims blamed the NCI for "an inexcusable delay in bringing this information to the attention of the American public."

The advocacy group urged the Clinton administration to hold a national public health conference to assess the risks and appropriate responses, and to warn people who were in the fallout path to get their thyroids checked.
